K–Ar datings for the sheeted dikes yield values of 79–84 and 95–102 Ma (Kravchenko-Berezhnoy & Nazimova 1991), suggesting that they are of Albian–Campanian age. The volcanic–siliceous complex is composed of tectonic blocks closely associated with the ophiolites. This complex consists of lava ﬂows, lava breccias, tuffs, and cherts. The volcanics are calc-alkaline basalts to basaltic andesites, that formed in an ensimatic island arc (Kravchenko- Berezhnoy 1989; Chekhovich et al . 1990; Kravchenko-Berezhnoy & Nazimova 1991). These rocks are dated as Senonian by the presence of inocerams, and as Campanian–Maastrichtian by radiolarians (Chekhovich et al. 1990). The volcanic–terrigenous complex forms a dis- continuous stripe of fault-bounded blocks extend- ing along the southeastern slope of the Central Range. The lower section of this complex (Khynkhlonai Formation), dominated by lavas and coarse to ﬁne tuffs, and the upper section (Krutogorskaya Formation) conformably overlies the lower formation and consists of arc-derived terrigenous rocks—graywacke, siltstone, mud- stone, sandstone, and tuffaceous varieties. In case of coincidence of the areas occupied by hard and soft components isolated in single-component and mul- ticomponent Zijderveld’s plots, these hard or soft components were grouped into a single population. All sequences were divided into blocks that com- prised either fault-bounded fragments of sections or fragments of sections with distinctive rock atti- tudes. The simplest model involves tilting of the sequences to the west-northwest and northwest directions by 45–65°. Such directions attitudes (in F1 blocks, rocks dip 45° at an azimuth of 185°; in VT3 blocks, rocks dip 30° at azimuths of 320, 100 and 60°; in VT2 blocks, rocks dip 25° at an azimuth of 230°, 15° at an azimuth of 150°, and 30° at an azimuth of 65°) and because they coexist with A vectors of both normal and reversed polarities, these components must be independent, rather than the result of summing different but equally stable components (e.g. A and secondary com- ponents of the ﬁrst two groups). Lastly , Group 4 includes hard A components isolated from the rocks of the volcanic–terrigenous complex. The fact that the A com- ponents show almost no horizontal rotation makes this model the most realistic. Because the mean B components for the blocks are equal in the geo- graphic reference frame, the studied sequences of the volcanic–terrigenous and ﬂysch complexes may have rotated as a single rigid slab, without signiﬁcant internal deformations. Tilting these structures back in an east-southeast direction to align their B component with the remagnetizing geomagnetic ﬁeld reveals that, prior to deforma- tion (which is recorded paleomagnetically), the sequences dipped steeply (50–80°) to the south- west. The directions of A components in the strati- graphic reference frame based on rock attitudes for that position remained virtually unchanged (A rot in Tables 2, 3), which further conﬁrms the hypothesis that the framework of Karaginsky Island arose without signiﬁcant rotations of its blocks. Paleomagnetic methods Standard collection and analysis methods were used throughout the study. About eight samples were col- lected per site with a gasoline powered drill. In some cases, when the rock was too friable, too fractured, or too hard to drill satisfactorily in the ﬁeld, hand samples were collected and cores drilled from them in the laboratory. Together the iron - and manganese -rich cycles constitute the Early Paleoproterozoic Hotazel Formation, with an age of ca. 2200 Ma (Cornell et al., 1996) or 2400 .Ma (Bau et al., 1999). It has previously been uncertain if hematite (I) and late diagenetic and/or metamorphic hausmannite (I) were consumed during this alteration, because both minerals occur widely in both altered and unaltered ores. The Mashonaland and Hartley igneous units are broadly coeval-possibly consanguineous with the poorly dated Sibasa basalt (Soutpansberg Group) and Sand River dikes (Barton and Pretorius, 1997)and related to the ca. 19 00 Ma rift stage of a Wilson cycle (Cornell et al., 1998). Our MAM -2 pole lies just beyond the Mashonaland and Hartley results along the apparent polar wander path (Fig. 6A; Evans et al., in press) and so may result from extension-related magmatism that ex pelled stratabound fluids into the Kalahari manganese field. Alternatively, MAM -2 could be due to foreland-driven orogenic fluids from the Kheis fold thrust episode (Gutzmer and Beukes, 1996), loosely dated at 1700 to 1800 Ma (Stowe, 1983; Cornell et al., 1998). Both the rift - and Kheis -related tectonic models for MAM -2 would be consistent with the various crosscutting relationships observed in the Kalahari manganese field (Gutzmer and Beukes, 1996). Existing regional crosscutting relationships and isotopic data from the Kalahari

sted a late Mesoproterozoic age for the Wessels event (Dixon, 1989), thereby associating it with tectonothermal activity in the Namaqua orogen (Gutzmer and Beukes, 1996). Our WESS paleomagnetic pole may help ref ine the age of Wessels hydrothermal aeration, through comparisons with previously determined, well-dated paleomagnetic poles from the Kalahari craton. Evans et al. (in press), following Onstott et al. (1986), summarized the existing database and determined a large loop of paleomagnetic poles that sweeps twice through northernmost Africa, at ca. 1240 and 1100 Ma (Fig. 6B). GFF , Vol. 123 (Pt. 4, December), pp. 205–215. Stockholm. ISSN 1103-5897. Abstract: The 1.85–1.67 Ga Transscandinavian Igneous Belt (TIB) forms a major Paleoproterozoic igneous complex in the western part of the Fennoscandian Shield. Different tectonic models propose that the TIB was formed in a tectonic regime governed either by compression or by extension. This paper presents an analysis of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) and paleomagnetic data from the Rätan granite (1.70 Ga), which forms a large pluton in the central part of the TIB. The major aim of the study is to test the existing tectonic models and to de- fine a paleomagnetic pole position for the Rätan granite. Three contrast- ing magnetic fabric domains are identified. In the eastern and western domains the AMS fabric is characterized by NW–SE to N–S trending subvertical foliation planes and a girdle distribution of the maximum and intermediate anisotropy axes. The central domain is characterized by subhorizontal magnetic foliation planes and lineations that cluster in a NW–SE trending direction. We

he central domain is characterized by subhorizontal magnetic foliation planes and lineations that cluster in a NW–SE trending direction. We suggest that the Rätan granite was emplaced in a tectonic regime governed by NW–SE directed extension and that the pluton was fed obliquely with a magma source situated to the present northwest. A positive baked contact test is demonstrated for a basic dyke suggesting that the Rätan granite has not been re-magnet- ized since c. 1.6 Ga. A paleomagnetic formation mean direction is de- fined for the granite (decl. = 2°, incl. = 59°) that yields a paleopole posi- tion of Plat = 67° and Plon = 190°. Revised manuscript accepted 23 August 2001. The Transscandinavian Igneous Belt (TIB) forms a major Late Paleoproterozoic igneous complex in the Fennoscandian Shield. The TIB was formed at c. 1.85–1.67 Ga (Ahl et al. 1999) along the southwestern boundary of the Svecofennian Domain (Gaál & Gorbatschev 1987). It defines a belt of igneous rocks that ex- tends

e-mar- gin process (e.g. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova 1993), and plate tectonic models proposed that the TIB was formed in a tectonic regime governed by compression (Windley 1993). However, Ahl et al. (1999) present a model suggesting that the Dala granit- oids in the central part of the TIB were formed in a period of tran- sition between subduction-related compression (1.81–1.77 Ga) and an extensive environment (1.70–1.68 Ga). The Rätan granite (e.g. Lundegårdh 1967; Lundqvist 1968), which forms a large intrusion north and east of the Dala granitoids, was emplaced at c. 1.70 Ga (U–Pb, Wilson et al. 1985; Patchett et al. 1987; Delin 1996). Sparse AMS data from the granite indicate that it may have formed in an extensive tectonic regime (Mattsson & Elming 2001). GFF , Vol. 123 (Pt. 4, December), pp. 205–215. Stockholm. ISSN 1103-5897. Abstract: The 1.85–1.67 Ga Transscandinavian Igneous Belt (TIB) forms a major Paleoproterozoic igneous complex in the western part of the Fennoscandian Shield. Different tectonic models propose that the TIB was formed in a tectonic regime governed either by compression or by extension. This paper presents an analysis of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) and paleomagnetic data from the Rätan granite (1.70 Ga), which forms a large pluton in the central part of the TIB. The major aim of the study is to test the existing tectonic models and to de- fine a paleomagnetic pole position for the Rätan granite. Three contrast- ing magnetic fabric domains are identified. In the eastern and western domains the AMS fabric is characterized by NW–SE to N–S trending subvertical foliation planes and a girdle distribution of the maximum and intermediate anisotropy axes. The central domain is characterized by subhorizontal magnetic foliation planes and lineations that cluster in a NW–SE trending direction. We suggest that the Rätan granite was emplaced in

The Tecomazuchil Formation was sampled in stratigraphic order over a total height of 13 m in 11 beds, and magnetostratigraphic results have already been published (Urrutia-Fucugauchi et al., 1990). Sampling was done in stratigraphic order, taking 3–4 cores per horizon to check for the internal consistency of the magnetic record. Conclusion of rock magnetic experiments The remanent magnetization of the Morelos lime- stone was carried by goethite and magnetite in variable proportions, with minor hematite. The Tecomazuchil Formation was sampled in stratigraphic order over a total height of 13 m in 11 beds, and magnetostratigraphic results have already been published (Urrutia-Fucugauchi et al., 1990). The Morelos Formation was sampled in 8 beds covering a total thickness of 18 m. Roughly 50 km further to the south, the Rosario Formation was sampled in 12 beds with a total thickness of 7 m. Here the overlaying Tecocoyunca Group has been studied as well, but the paleomagnetic results showed strong, unremovable secondary overprints and were therefore of no tectonic relevance (Bo ¨hnel, 1985). The rocks were sampled using a portable gasoline- powered drill with diamond drill bits, and the cores were oriented in situ with an inclinometer and a mag- netic compass (Collinson, 1983). Sampling was done in stratigraphic order, taking 3–4 cores per horizon to check for the internal consistency of the magnetic record. In this manner 31 cores from the Morelos lime- stone were obtained, 38 cores from the Tecomazuchil sandstone, and 35 cores from the Rosario Formation. IRM acquisition IRM acquisition and back-ﬁeld demagnetization curves are shown in Fig. 5. None of the samples was saturated by the maximum available ﬁeld of 1.5 T. This was due to the presence of highly coercive mag- netic minerals like goethite or hematite, as suggested above. The inﬂection of the IRM acquisition and back-ﬁeld demagnetization curves at ﬁelds <200 mT again indicated the presence of magnetite. 3.1.5. Conclusion of rock magnetic experiments The remanent magnetization of the Morelos lime- stone was carried by goethite and magnetite in variable proportions, with minor hematite. The Tecomazuchil and Rosario sandstones contained the same minerals, but hematite in the form of pigment and specularite was present in larger concentrations in many samples. In both of these formations, the magnetic mineralogy was fairly constant within each bed, and changes occurred predominantly between di erent beds. This may be the result of varying conditions during the de- position of the sediments, but also of local di erences of recent weathering of the rock which produced more or less goethite. 3.2. This was done up to 420 8C for the Morelos limestones, as at this temperature, the NRM had dropped to a level comparable to the noise of the SQUID-magnetometer. Nevertheless, up to that tem- perature the directional variation of remanence was mainly uni-vectorial and the demagnetization curves tended towards the origin of the diagram [Fig. 6(a)]. It was therefore straightforward to determine character- istic remanence (ChRM) directions for 27 out of 31 samples. Vector plots for the Tecomazuchil sandstone were pretty varied: many samples showed uni-vectorial NRM [Fig. 6(c)]. This was always the case for samples containing magnetite and hematite (specularite), which supports the idea that both minerals carried the same, possibly primary, remanence. Other samples contained at least two remanence components [Fig. 6(b),(d)], and sometimes the demagnetization process did not isolate a stable endpoint ChRM [Fig. 6(b)]. This happened more often in samples where goethite dominated the magnetic properties. Finally, a few samples showed stable endpoint ChRM, but of intermediate direction. All in all, a total of 11 samples from the Tecomazuchil sandstone had to be rejected for further interpret- ations. The recent acquisition of paleomagnetic data from Paleozoic rocks of this region, albeit still scarce, permit establishment of some constrains on the tectonic and paleogeographic evolution of some of these terranes. A reliable paleomagnetic pole from the Early Cambrian Cerro Totora Formation in northern Precordillera confirms that the Argentine Precordillera is an exotic terrane that was part of or adjacent to Laurentia, very likely at the Ouachita Embayment, in the Early Cambrian. Paleomag- netic poles from an Early Ordovician magmatic belt in northwest Argentina permit the identification of a peri-Gondwanic–rotated terrane, called the Eastern Puna–Famatina terrane, with volcanic arc affinities. Early Paleozoic paleomagnetic poles from the Western Puna (Sierra de Almeida, Chile) were previously interpreted as evidence of a para-autochthonous nature of the Arequipa-Antofalla Massif that rotated successively clockwise and counter

Until very recently, no paleomagnetic data were available to test and constrain the tectonic models mentioned before. This was due, in part to the few paleomagnetic studies carried out on this region, but also to an apparently widespread and pervasive Permian remagnetizing event that inhibited determination of the primary magnetic components from many of the Lower Paleozoic rocks (Rapalini and Tarling, 1993; Truco and Rapalini, 1996). A successful paleomagnetic study was recently carried out on the Lower Cambrian Cerro Totora Formation (Rapalini and Astini, 1998), exposed in the northern Precordillera (location 1 in Fig. 1). The Cerro Totora Formation consists in a mixed suc- cession of evaporites, red siliciclastics, and carbonates (Astini and Vaccari, 1996) with trilobites of the Bonnia-Olenellus zone (Vaccari, 1990). This succession has been interpreted as typical synrift deposits (Astini and Vaccari, 1996), possibly accumulated during the initial rifting of the Argentine Precordillera from the Ouachita embayment of south-central North America (Thomas and Astini, 1996). The Fen Central Complex, along with associated intrusions, were emplaced during minor extensional activity that occurred after continental separation between Baltica and Laurentia. This interpretation is consistent with our 580 Ma paleoreconstruction, which shows that Baltica had rifted and rotated from its 615 Ma position adjacent to Greenland. We interpret the ages and the tectonics to re¯ect opening of an ocean basin from north to south during the latest Neoproterozoic to earliest Paleozoic time (615±540 Ma). The polarity option for the Fen pole remains an important and open question due to recent suggestions of a true polar wander event in the mid- Cambrian; however, we consider that the south polarity option offers the simplest tectonic model for the rifting of Rodinia and opening of the Iapetus Ocean between Baltica and Laurentia. Finally, we note the similarity of the Fen paleomagnetic pole to paleomagnetic poles of Permo-Triassic age in Baltica and urge caution in the unequivocal use of the Fen pole as primary until further substantiated by coeval poles from Baltica. Eide,2 and Sven Dahlgren 3 Department of Geography and Geology, Indiana State University, Terre Haute, IN 47809 ABSTRACT The Fen Central Complex (FCC) and associated satellite dikes of the Fen Province in southern Norway record a magne- tization dating to 583 Ma. The paleomagnetic pole calculated from these rocks falls at 56 ° N, 150° E (dp 5 7°,d m 5 10°) and compares favorably with two previous investigations. The mean inclination in our study is slightly steeper than that of one of the earlier studies and we attribute this to the fact that previous investigators inadvertently sampled younger (late Paleozoic/early Mesozoic) dikes in the area. The age of the Fen paleomagnetic pole is constrained by two consistent 40Ar/ 39Ar ages from these rocks, which average 583 6 15 Ma, along with previously published ages ranging from 523±601 Ma. The Fen Central Complex, along with associated intrusions, were emplaced during minor extensional activity that occurred after continental separation between Baltica and Laurentia. This interpretation is consistent with our 580 Ma paleoreconstruction, which shows that Baltica had rifted and rotated from its 615 Ma position adjacent to Greenland. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: 9 Beijing, China Received 1 May 1997; accepted 22 September 1998 Abstract This study has investigated magnetic remanence, rock magnetism and anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) in granulite and amphibolite grade metamorphic terranes of the Huabei Shield between Inner Mongolia in the west and the Bohai Sea in the east. Rock magnetic studies identify annealed metamorphic magnetite grains with multidomain properties as the remanence carriers; a widely recorded stable remanence was probably ﬁxed by grain shape e ects. Granulite facies terranes are typically between one and two orders more strongly magnetised than amphibolite terranes and AMS fabrics correlate mostly with metamorphic mineral fabrics observed in the country rocks. Progressive thermal demagnetisation identiﬁes a range of two and three component structures resident in magnetite. An important component recognised as a partial or complete remagnetisation by Late Mesozoic–Tertiary tectonic/magmatic activity is present in basement at the southern margin of the outcrop (Miyun terrane) and where extensive granite plutonism has occurred (Zhunhua terrane). These components have directions corresponding to remanence in the Yunmeng Shan Granite (119–114 Ma, D/I = 33/58 8, 39 samples, a 95 = 3.58, palaeopole at 2018E, 64 8N).

Study of magnetic susceptibility at low temperatures (KLT analysis) cools the rock to the temperature of liquid nitrogen ( ÿ1968C) and records susceptibility during subsequent return to room temperature. The susceptibility of multi-domain (MD) grains is con- trolled mainly by magnetocrystalline anisotropy (Uyeda et al., 1963) which is strongly temperature dependent: magnetite undergoes a structural change known as the Verwey transition at ÿ1508C. At this point the magnetocrystalline anisotropy constant, k1,i s minimised; a peak in susceptibility near this tempera- ture is diagnostic of MD magnetite and deﬁnes Group 3 behaviour of Senanayake and McElhinny (1981). Provided that grain elongation is >10%, single domain (SD) grain susceptibility is dominated by shape anisotropy which produces preferential magneti- sation along the length of an elongate grain to mini- mise magnetostatic energy (Pullaiah et al., 1975). Medium to high grade polymetamorphic terranes occur along the northern margin of the Huabei (North China) Shield as inliers exposed beneath supracrustal successions comprising the Meso-Neoproterozoic Jixian Supergroup. Cooling of these terranes and their elevation to present surface levels occurred prior to de- position of the oldest part of the Jixian succession at 01850 Ma. The remanence must however, have been acquired after the last stages of ductile deformation which occurred within the interval 2500–2200 Ma because regional temperatures were then above the Curie point. A sampling site com- prises between seven and twenty two 2.4 cm diameter cores distributed across at least several metres of out- crop (e.g. Fig. 7). Cores were oriented in situ by sun and magnetic compasses and cut into 2.2 cm length cylinders for magnetic measurements. Introduction Although the kinematics of the major Shields during Precambrian times is quantiﬁed by palaeomagnetic study, the recoverable record is always incomplete, both because the rock record is itself only sporadically preserved, and because later overprinting can obscure an ancient remanence record. The present Precambrian palaeomagnetic database is mostly derived from study of intense, but generally brief, igneous episodes and platformal successions of Meso- and Neoproterozoic age. The oldest palaeomagnetic record in each shield is preserved in the underlying basement rocks. This base- ment typically comprises a polymetamorphic gneiss complex produced by crustal accretion and repeated reworking during Archaean and Early Proterozoic times. s is a bulk parameter recording preferred mineral orientation by metamorphic crystallisation and/or ﬂow mechan- isms. The grains contributing to this e ect have para- magnetic and ferromagnetic properties; the paramagnetic minerals are mostly the iron-bearing sili- cates whilst the ferromagnetic contribution is from magnetite, and sometimes pyrrhotite or hematite. The strong ferromagnetic e ect of the small volume of these latter grains is often much larger than the para- magnetic and (weak negative) diamagnetic e ects of the bulk silicate matrix. Whilst the inﬂuence of fabric on the dilute amounts of ferromagnetic grains in which the stable remanence resides cannot be isolated by study of AMS, it is a useful qualitative indicator of bias of magnetic remanence by fabric; a comparison between results from samples of strong and weak fab- rics at the same site is often able to recognise the likely importance of any such bias. Following cessation of volcanism, a transgressing sea deposited limestones, shales, mudstones and greywackes between Late Caradoc and Ludlow times. This succession forms the Winderemere Supergroup and makes up the Silurian outcrop in Figure 1. During burial and subsequent Acadian deformation the Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Lake District were metamorphosed to no higher than lower greenschist grade, in common with the paratectonic Caledonides of Wales; this was insucient to comprehensively remagnetize pre-Acadian rocks which are reported widely to retain an Ordovician remanence record (Briden and Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978; Piper, 1979; Channell and McCabe, 1992). Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. The intrusions tend to be magnetically less stable than equivalent volcanics (Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978, the Carrock Fell Layered Gabbros are a notable exception) probably because they are more commonly dominated by larger magnetite grain sizes and multi domains. Higher failure rates therefore accompany these studies and some samples have a remanence dominated by Recent ﬁeld components. Nevertheless, numerous intrusive igneous samples show a coherent remanence structure unobscured by Variscan or later overprinting and it is with these components that the present study is primarily concerned. Palaeomagnetic study of intrusive igneous rocks, including application of thermal demagnet- ization, ﬁeld tests and principal component analysis, identiﬁes a history of Ordovician to Devonian magnetization. Late plutons (Shap and Skiddaw granites and/or aureoles) record a shallow dipolar (A3) axis (mean declination/inclination (D=I 278= 178) dating from emplacement in late Early Devonian times ( c. 395 Ma). Although this axis is recorded as a sporadic overprint in older rocks, no pervasive remagnetization is attributable to batholith emplacement. Instead, the Carrock Fell Complex Layered Gabbros have a mid- to late Ordovician (A1) remanence ( D=I 174=ÿ 5818, 36 samples, a95  488) predating regional F2 folding. Later events in this igneous complex comprise the Carrock Fell Granophyre with a post-folding Ordovician remanence, and Round Knott Dolerite with a remanence linked to hydrothermal alteration late in the Ordovician magmatic episode. A Late Ordovician (Ashgill) palaeoﬁeld is also deﬁned by remanence (A2) in the Threlkeld–St John’s Microgranite and aureole (438 Ma, D=I 2365=6338, 41 samples, a95  478). he ﬁnal phase of subduction-related magmatism at this margin of Avalonia. Following cessation of volcanism, a transgressing sea deposited limestones, shales, mudstones and greywackes between Late Caradoc and Ludlow times. This succession forms the Winderemere Supergroup and makes up the Silurian outcrop in Figure 1. During burial and subsequent Acadian deformation the Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Lake District were metamorphosed to no higher than lower greenschist grade, in common with the paratectonic Caledonides of Wales; this was insucient to comprehensively remagnetize pre-Acadian rocks which are reported widely to retain an Ordovician remanence record (Briden and Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978; Piper, 1979; Channell and McCabe, 1992). In addition to the basic plutonism noted above, acidic magmatism occurred at various stages between the intense mid-Ordovician volcanic events and the culmination of tectonic activity in the Acadian episode. A general distinction is recognized between earlier Na-rich activity and later more K-rich activity (Piper et al., 1978). ents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. The Carrock Fell Complex was the subject of earlier study employing a.f. demagnetization and endpoint analysis (Briden and Morris, 1973; Morris, 1973). Since the complex was then considered to be a post-tectonic event, the data were evaluated in situ; more recent evidence shows that the layered gabbros predate F2 folding (Roberts, 1971; Harris and Dagger, 1987). Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. The same motion is recognized in contemporaneous data from the Welsh Caledonides where declinations are rotated by c.5 5 8 relative to contemporaneous results from the Lake District. Adjustment for this (probable late Acadian) rotation beings fold trends of the Paratectonic Caledonides into alignment and identiﬁes a parallel mid- to late Ordovician destructive plate margin comprising forearc (Lake District) and backarc (North Wales). This arc was oriented latitudinally in mid-southerly latitudes during formation and the bulk of the magmatism occurred during a single normal-polarity chron. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Three episodes of folding (F1–F3) have been recognized in the Skiddaw Slate Group immediately to the south of the Carrock Fell Complex by Roberts (1971). ecognized close to the intrusive contact with the Skiddaw Granite (sites 1 and 2 in Figure 12). At greater distances from the granite contact components deﬁned by thermal demagnetization reﬂect the overprinting e ects of the granite and are more prominent in this body than in the Layered Gabbros or Granophyre (Figure 14). Other samples have a SSW ChRM following removal of a present ﬁeld component (sample 3-4 in Figure 13). This is magnetite-held like the granite overprints and, since it is also close to the Early Carboniferous palaeoﬁeld direction, cannot positively be identiﬁed as older than the granite. However, overprinting of this age is not recognized elsewhere in the region; furthermore four samples illustrate a reversal in this component (sample 5-5 in Figure 13). Whilst intrusion ages are uncertain, an origin related to emplacement with, or soon after, the granophyre is probable because they are not observed in the younger Eskdale Granite. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. he ﬁnal phase of subduction-related magmatism at this margin of Avalonia. Following cessation of volcanism, a transgressing sea deposited limestones, shales, mudstones and greywackes between Late Caradoc and Ludlow times. This succession forms the Winderemere Supergroup and makes up the Silurian outcrop in Figure 1. During burial and subsequent Acadian deformation the Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Lake District were metamorphosed to no higher than lower greenschist grade, in common with the paratectonic Caledonides of Wales; this was insucient to comprehensively remagnetize pre-Acadian rocks which are reported widely to retain an Ordovician remanence record (Briden and Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978; Piper, 1979; Channell and McCabe, 1992). In addition to the basic plutonism noted above, acidic magmatism occurred at various stages between the intense mid-Ordovician volcanic events and the culmination of tectonic activity in the Acadian episode. A general distinction is recognized between earlier Na-rich activity and later more K-rich activity (Piper et al., 1978). Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. We report U–Pb ages and palaeomagnetic results for two suites of maﬁc sills within the intracratonic Bangemall Basin of Western Australia, one of which is dated at 1070 ± 6 Ma and carries a high-stability palaeomagnetic remanence. Comparison of the Bangemall palaeopole with Laurentian data suggests that previous reconstructions of eastern Australia against either western Canada (SWEAT) or the western United States (AUSWUS) are not viable at 1070 Ma. This implies that the Paciﬁc Ocean did not form by separation of Australia–Antarc- tica from Laurentia, and that up to 10 000 km of late Neoproterozoic passive margins need to be matched with other continental blocks within any proposed Rodinia supercontinent. We report U–Pb ages and palaeomagnetic results for two suites of maﬁc sills within the intracratonic Bangemall Basin of Western Australia, one of which is dated at 1070 ± 6 Ma and carries a high-stability palaeomagnetic remanence. Comparison of the Bangemall palaeopole with Laurentian data suggests that previous reconstructions of eastern Australia against either western Canada (SWEAT) or the western United States (AUSWUS) are not viable at 1070 Ma. This implies that the Paciﬁc Ocean did not form by separation of Australia–Antarc- tica from Laurentia, and that up to 10 000 km of late Neoproterozoic passive margins need to be matched with other continental blocks within any proposed Rodinia supercontinent. Our results permit a reconstruction (AUSMEX) that closely aligns late Mesoproterozoic orogenic belts in north-east Australia and southernmost Laurentia. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: iversity, Kobe 657-8501, Japan Received 27 May 2001; received in revised form 20 September 2001; accepted 13 October 2001 Abstract We report paleomagnetic results for Carboniferous rocks from the eastern part of the Hexi Corridor, which we have demonstrated to be the western extension of the North China block (NCB). The characteristic high-temperature remanence component (B-component) exhibits predominantly reverse polarity, and is generally separable by thermal demagnetization temperature steps between 350 and 580‡C. This B-component can also be isolated by alternating fields (AFs) cleaning at a peak value of 20^30 mT using a hybrid thermal^AF demagnetization method. The B-component shows a positive fold test at the 95% confidence level, indicating that it was acquired before Late Triassic to Early Jurassic folding. We interpret the B-component to be of primary origin acquired during the Carboniferous. The corresponding pole positions are at 14.0‡E, 10.5‡N, K95 = 6.2‡ for the Early-Middle Carboniferous (late Visean to Namurian) and at 10.2‡E, 33.3‡N, K95 = 16.7‡ for the Late Carboniferous (Stephanian). Two major folding events occurred, presumably during the Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous and during the Early Ju- rassic to Middle Jurassic, corresponding to the Variscan and Indosinian orogenies, respectively. Indeed, two unconformities can be distinguished in the Alashan/Hexi Corridor terrane, the earlier one between Late Devonian and Early Carbon- iferous sediments, and the later one between Early Jurassic and Middle Jurassic sediments [17]. The Carboniferous system is made up in as- cending order of the Lower Carboniferous Chou- niugou Formation, Middle Carboniferous Jin- gyuan and Yanghugou Formations, and the Upper Carboniferous Taiyuan Formation (Fig. 2). The Lower Carboniferous series unconform- ably overlies the Upper Devonian Zhongning Formation. It is mainly composed of sandy sand- stone and mudstone interbedded with limestone or light-gray and gray limestone. The upper part of this series yields corals (e.g. Yuanophyllum kan- suense, Dibunophyllum bristolens ), brachiopods (Gigantoproductus maxima , Kansuella kansuensis ) and £ora (e.g. Sublepidodendron mirabile , Rhodea hsianghsiangensis), indicating a late Datang age (i.e. late Visean stage, [17]). Two major folding events occurred, presumably during the Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous and during the Early Ju- rassic to Middle Jurassic, corresponding to the Variscan and Indosinian orogenies, respectively. Indeed, two unconformities can be distinguished in the Alashan/Hexi Corridor terrane, the earlier one between Late Devonian and Early Carbon- iferous sediments, and the later one between Early Jurassic and Middle Jurassic sediments [17]. The Carboniferous system is made up in as- cending order of the Lower Carboniferous Chou- niugou Formation, Middle Carboniferous Jin- gyuan and Yanghugou Formations, and the Upper Carboniferous Taiyuan Formation (Fig. 2). The Lower Carboniferous series unconform- ably overlies the Upper Devonian Zhongning Formation. It is mainly composed of sandy sand- stone and mudstone interbedded with limestone or light-gray and gray limestone. The upper part of this series yields corals (e.g. Yuanophyllum kan- suense, Dibunophyllum bristolens ), brachiopods (Gigantoproductus maxima , Kansuella kansuensis ) and £ora (e.g. Sublepidodendron mirabile , Rhodea hsianghsiangensis), indicating a late Datang age (i.e. late Visean stage, [17]). Therefore, the bulk sample experiences far less heating than in convention- al experiments and, consequently, alteration is greatly reduced (e.g. [4]). The microwave/SQUID magnetometer system at Liverpool University, op- erating at a microwave frequency of 8.2 GHz, has been used successfully for palaeointensity studies using ceramics [5,6] and historic lava [4,7]. The NCB was probably independent in terms of dynamics. its drift history was dominant by latitudinal placement ac- companying rotation in the Early Paleozoic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was part of Gondwanaland, and might be close to the YZB and Australia in the Early Paleozoic. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. During Late Permian to Late Triassic, the NCB and YZB were characterized by northern latitudinal placement and ro- tation on the pivot in the Dabie area. The NCB and YZB collided first in the eastern part where they were located at northern latitude of about 6"-8', and a triangular oceanic basin remained in the Late Permian. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was part of Gondwanaland, and might be close to the YZB and Australia in the Early Paleozoic. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic. APWPs for the three blocks have become consistent since the Late Jurassic, showing that they have completely sutured and no obvious relative displacement exists between them. It should be emphasized that kinematics and dynamics histo- ry revealed by APWPs are reflected by both the systematic drift history of blocks before collision and crust shortening and relative rotation after suturing. The NCB was probably independent in terms of dynamics. its drift history was dominant by latitudinal placement ac- companying rotation in the Early Paleozoic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was part of Gondwanaland, and might be close to the YZB and Australia in the Early Paleozoic. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. During Late Permian to Late Triassic, the NCB and YZB were characterized by northern latitudinal placement and ro- tation on the pivot in the Dabie area. The NCB and YZB collided first in the eastern part where they were located at northern latitude of about 6"-8', and a triangular oceanic basin remained in the Late Permian. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic. VOI. 41 supp. SCIENCE IN CHINA (Series D) December 1998 Paleomagnetic result of the Lower-Cretaceous from Luanping basin, Hebei Province and its tectonic implications * SUN Zhiming (M\%Pfl), YANG Zhenyu (@jEZ), MA Xinghua (qEq) and ZHAO Yue ( & &!4) (Institute of Geomechanics, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing 100081, China) Received September 16, 1998 Abstract A paleomagnetic study of about 95 samples from 16 sites sampled in the Early Cretaceous in Luanping basin in Hebei Province was reported. Stepwise thermal demagnetization was used to isolate magnetic components. Most samples have a characteristic direction with a high temperature component above 50093 . The tectonic-corrected data are D = 347.8'. I = 50.4'. ass = 7. lo, and the corresponding pole position is at 76. ION, 346.3'E, with dp = 6.4". dm = 3.8', paleolatitude A = 31.1°N. This result indicates a counterclockwise post-Cretaceous rotation of 30.7" + 9.8" with respect to the stable Ordos basin in the west of North China Block, and a non-significant northward mo- tion. This rotation could be related to local fault action or structural detachment, or regional NNW-NWWward motion and collision of Kula-Pacific plate with eastern China since the Early Cret

This rotation could be related to local fault action or structural detachment, or regional NNW-NWWward motion and collision of Kula-Pacific plate with eastern China since the Early Cretaceous. Keywords: Luanping basin, Early Cretaceous, counterclockwise rotation, Kula-Pacific plate. Since the 1980s, a large number of paleomagnetic studies have been carried out in the Ordos basin in the west of North China Block (NCB)['-~]. A number of reliable Jurassic-Cretaceous pa- leomagnetic data have been obtained to establish the apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the whole NCB, and to provide important fundamental information for studying its structural evolu- tion. A lot of geological studies have shown the distinct tectonic differential movement between the eastern and western part of NCB since the Mesozoic. The western part of NCB is character- ized by large Jurassic-Cretaceous fault basin, while the eastern part is characterized by small Mid- dle Jurassic-Cretaceous fault basin, large scale magmatic explosion and intrusion, and severe struc- tural activity. So, paleomagnetic studies may contribute to a better understanding of the Mesozoic evolution of NCB by correlating the Jurassic-Cretaceous paleomagnetic data with that from other tectonic units. A c

nding of the Mesozoic evolution of NCB by correlating the Jurassic-Cretaceous paleomagnetic data with that from other tectonic units. A considerable amount of paleomagnetic studies have been carried out in the Juras- sic-Cretaceous sediments in the eastern part of NCB. It is difficult to interpret the paleomagnetic data because of the complex structure, multi-periodic volcanic activity and widespread remagneti- zation related to the Yanshannian orogeny in this region. In this paper we report the paleomagnet- ic result obtained from lower Cretaceous sediments in Luanping basin, and discuss its tectonic im- plications by comparison with paleomagnetic results from adjacent blocks. 1 Sampling and paleomagnetic measurements The Luanping basin is one of the regions in NCB in which the late Jurassic-early Cretaceous volcanic sediments are well developed. The Peri Rhyolite has been correlated with the Eastons Arm Rhyolite of the southern Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11). The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006 2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag- netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified (Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’). This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite, which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with the Peri Rhyolite. In contrast, Opdyke et al. (2000), follow- ing earlier workers (Hocking 1973; Stroud 1990b), regarded this Boomi Creek succession as a minor thrust sliver belonging to the Caroda Formation. The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000) near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). A SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 310.6/H110064.0 Ma indicates a late Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6). Sampling of the middle Visean to Westphalian– Stephanian volcanic-rich succession of the Rocky Creek Block (64 sites, 734 samples) has been carried out in three phases. Reconnaissance sampling (17 sites, 171 samples) was carried out in 1987. The Peri Rhyolite has been correlated with the Eastons Arm Rhyolite of the southern Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11). The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006 2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag- netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified (Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’). This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite, which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with the Peri Rhyolite. In contrast, Opdyke et al. (2000), follow- ing earlier workers (Hocking 1973; Stroud 1990b), regarded this Boomi Creek succession as a minor thrust sliver belonging to the Caroda Formation. y Creek Conglomerate, such as the Hazelvale Rhyolite in the lower part of the formation. The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000) near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). A SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 310.6/H110064.0 Ma indicates a late Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6). The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. Sampling of the middle Visean to Westphalian– Stephanian volcanic-rich succession of the Rocky Creek Block (64 sites, 734 samples) has been carried out in three phases. Reconnaissance sampling (17 sites, 171 samples) was carried out in 1987. Extensive follow-up sampling (41 sites, 492 samples) was carried out in 1995 for comprehensive stratigraphic coverage of the successions and for fold tests. The potential of magnetic fabric analysis for determin- ation of transport directions in ignimbrites and trans- ported air-fall tuffs has been well established from pioneering studies on felsic volcanic rocks, mainly Cenozoic, in southwestern North America (MacDonald & Palmer 1990; Palmer et al. 1991). Such studies have shown that the K min axis of the AMS ellipsoid generally represents the pole to the foliation or flow-banding plane, that the K max axis parallels the flow- or transport-axis, and that imbrication of coarser components within the volcanic rocks can be used as an indication of transport direction with the source expected in the downdip direction of imbrication. The method can only be applied reliably if it can be established that the AMS ellipsoids reflect primary depositional patterns and not tectonic deformation. The in situ K max axes of the volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks of the Rocky Creek Block show an overall north– south alignment (Figure 10b). The regional tectonic grain is also north–south (Figures 3, 4) and a tectonic origin of the AMS pattern might, therefore, be surmised at first glance. INTERPRETATION Overprint magnetisations: post-folding MIDDLE–LATE CENOZOIC OVERPRINTS A magnetically soft overprint of exclusively normal polarity and with in situ directions close to the present local field direction is consistently present throughout the sites (Figure 12a, b). This component is unblocked at temperatures up to 300°C and in alternating fields up to 30 mT . Its mean direction is indistinguishable from a present field component in the southward adjacent Werrie Block. Both are similar to an overprint observed on the south coast of New South Wales and interpreted as Early Miocene in age (Nott et al. 1991). This set of over- prints may be indicative of a regional mid-Tertiary weathering event, although the overprints’ exclusive normal polarity and closeness to the present local field direction alternatively may point to a recent viscous origin. SAMPLING Sampling strategy An initial pilot study of the Tamworth Belt succession, on the Lower Carboniferous volcano-sedimentary succession of the Upper Rouchel region, demonstrated that ignimbritic volcanics can retain their primary magnetisation, despite conditions leading to pervasive overprinting of inter- calated volcaniclastic rocks. Widespread occurrence of magnetic overprints of Permo-Carboniferous (Schmidt 1988; Klootwijk 1996b) and Permo-Triassic age (Lackie & Schmidt 1993) throughout the Tamworth Belt succession and the Carboniferous succession of the Texas and Coffs Harbour Oroclines (Aubourg et al. 1994) has become well established. Therefore, sampling of the Rocky Creek Block concentrated on the frequent volcanic and tuff-rich volcani- clastic intercalations—ash-flow tuffs, ash-fall tuffs, lavas, tuffites—throughout the upper Lower to Upper Carbon- iferous succession. Reconnaissance sampling (17 sites, 171 samples) was carried out in 1987. Preliminary palaeomagnetic results from this collection were listed in Klootwijk (1996a) and their implications were discussed in an initial syn- thesis of the Carboniferous palaeomagnetism of the Tamworth Belt (Klootwijk 1996b). Extensive follow-up sampling (41 sites, 492 samples) was carried out in 1995 for comprehensive stratigraphic coverage of the successions and for fold tests. These may have induced magnetic overprints on the studied successions of the Rocky Creek Block, requir- ing careful analysis and interpretation of the palaeo- magnetic data in order to separate and identify primary and overprint components, and perhaps incompletely cleaned pseudo-components. Top and bottom of the specimens were ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen per sample. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: . Well-defined triaxial ellipsoids are also prominent, but various sites do not have a clear magnetic fabric pattern. The potential of magnetic fabric analysis for determin- ation of transport directions in ignimbrites and trans- ported air-fall tuffs has been well established from pioneering studies on felsic volcanic rocks, mainly Cenozoic, in southwestern North America (MacDonald & Palmer 1990; Palmer et al. 1991). Such studies have shown that the K min axis of the AMS ellipsoid generally represents the pole to the foliation or flow-banding plane, that the K max axis parallels the flow- or transport-axis, and that imbrication of coarser components within the volcanic rocks can be used as an indication of transport direction with the source expected in the downdip direction of imbrication. The method can only be applied reliably if it can be established that the AMS ellipsoids reflect primary depositional patterns and not tectonic deformation. The in situ K max axes of the volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks of the Rocky Creek Block show an overall north– south alignment (Figure 10b). The regional tectonic grain is also north–south (Figures 3, 4) and a tectonic origin of the AMS pattern might, therefore, be surmised at first glance. This component is unblocked at temperatures up to 300°C and in alternating fields up to 30 mT . Therefore, sampling of the Rocky Creek Block concentrated on the frequent volcanic and tuff-rich volcani- clastic intercalations—ash-flow tuffs, ash-fall tuffs, lavas, tuffites—throughout the upper Lower to Upper Carbon- iferous succession. Palaeomagnetic, rock magnetic and magnetic fabric results are presented for a Carboniferous (Visean to Westphalian) succession of felsic, mainly ignimbritic, volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks from the Rocky Creek Block of the northern Tamworth Belt, southern New England Orogen. Detailed thermal demagnetisation of 734 samples from 64 sites show three groups of magnetic components with low (<300°C), intermediate (300–600°C) and high (500–680°C) unblocking temperature ranges. Well-defined primary magnetisations have been determined for 28 sites with evidence of four overprint phases. The overprints arise from a mid-Tertiary weathering event (or possibly recent viscous origin), and from fluid movements associated with the Late Cretaceous opening of the Tasman Sea, thrusting during the Middle Triassic main phase of the Hunter–Bowen Orogeny, and latest Carboniferous – Early Permian formation of the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system. The Peri Rhyolite has been correlated with the Eastons Arm Rhyolite of the southern Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11). The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006 2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag- netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified (Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’). This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite, which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with the Peri Rhyolite. In contrast, Opdyke et al. (2000), follow- ing earlier workers (Hocking 1973; Stroud 1990b), regarded this Boomi Creek succession as a minor thrust sliver belonging to the Caroda Formation. The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. Deformation phases The New England Orogen has a long history of tectonic activity . Up to eight tectonic phases have been identified for the period from Devonian to the Late Cretaceous opening of the Tasman Sea (Korsch & Harrington 1981; Harrington & Korsch 1985a; Veevers et al. 1994b; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Tamworth Belt has been affected strongly by four of the phases. These may have induced magnetic overprints on the studied successions of the Rocky Creek Block, requir- ing careful analysis and interpretation of the palaeo- magnetic data in order to separate and identify primary and overprint components, and perhaps incompletely cleaned pseudo-components. The oldest of these four Carboniferous tectonic phases relates to development of the erosional disconformity between the lower and upper succession. Magnetic over- prints close to the top of the eroded succession may result from chemical processes during erosion, or may be due to fluid-flow that used the erosional disconformity as a pathway . The second tectonic phase had a major effect on the shape of the New England Orogen. MAGNETIC TREATMENT, ANALYSIS AND INTERPRETATION METHODS Sample preparation All core samples were sandblasted to remove possible mag- netic contamination from the stainless-steel drill barrels, and were sliced into standard specimens, 2.54 cm diameter and 2.2 cm height. Top and bottom of the specimens were ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen per sample. Alternating-field (AF) demagnetisation was carried out on one representative specimen per site and rock magnetic studies on one other specimen per site. Palaeomagnetic treatment One specimen per sample was subjected to progressive thermal demagnetisation in 18–36 steps up to peak temper- atures of 695°C. Thermal demagnetisation was carried out in large-volume furnaces (McElhinny et al. 1971) at the centre of feedback-controlled Rubens–Helmholtz coil systems (10 coils), which reduce the ambient magnetic field to less than 5 nT over the heating–cooling cycle. The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000) near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). A SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 310.6/H110064.0 Ma indicates a late Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6). The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. Widespread occurrence of magnetic overprints of Permo-Carboniferous (Schmidt 1988; Klootwijk 1996b) and Permo-Triassic age (Lackie & Schmidt 1993) throughout the Tamworth Belt succession and the Carboniferous succession of the Texas and Coffs Harbour Oroclines (Aubourg et al. 1994) has become well established. Therefore, sampling of the Rocky Creek Block concentrated on the frequent volcanic and tuff-rich volcani- clastic intercalations—ash-flow tuffs, ash-fall tuffs, lavas, tuffites—throughout the upper Lower to Upper Carbon- iferous succession. Top and bottom of the specimens were ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen per sample. ate Triassic paleomagnetic studies are required for the Yangtze Block as well as for the NCB. Post-Late Triassic paleomagnetic poles have been computed for areas spread over the Yangtze Block [2,7^9]. The northwestern and southwestern parts of this block were subjected to Cenozoic intra-cratonic deformation [10^12], and paleo- magnetic poles from these areas can not be re- garded as representative of the stable block. It is therefore necessary to establish a characteristic paleomagnetic pole from a tectonically stable part of the Yangtze Block, in order to understand its relationship to the NCB. We have focused in this study on Late Jurassic formations from the Sichuan basin that is consid- ered to be a stable part of the Yangtze Block. Brief reviews and some geodynamic interpretation of the development of this region are given by Zubkov et al. (1989) and Ashchepkov et al. (1995). A ring of Mesozoic - Cenozoic alkaline-basalt volcanism has been found at the northern margin Minusinsk Depression. The volcanic pipes and dikes arc grouped over the margins of Kopievo dome-shaped uplift and located near flexures and main faults (Fig.1). These volcanic bodies represent the root system of volcanic eruptions, forming volcanic pipes of complex structure, lava necks and numerous dikes. Pipes mostly are multiphase structures composed of eruptive breccias with altered groundmass containing abundant debris of basalts and hypabyssal basanites. No cover facies have been identified. Despite textural variety of the basalts, their chemical composition remains constant, and they are all classed as basanites. The volcanic rocks have been intruded into Devonian- Carboniferous age terrigenous deposits. The K-Ar isotopic ages (Zubkov et al., 1989) for these four volcanic pipes are found within the range of 71-45 Ma. Two volcanoes (Bele and Tergeshskaya pipes), 545 546 V.Yu. Davidson a aSchool of Geology and Geophysics, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK 73119, USA bDepartment of Geology and Petroleum Geology, University of Aberdeen, King’s College, Aberdeen AB24 3UE Scotland, UK Abstract Paleomagnetic results suggest that there was a ﬂuid-ﬂow event which caused dolomitization and hematite authigenesis in serpentinite within the Highland Border Group along the Highland Boundary Fault in central Scotland in the late Carboniferous/ early Permian. Geochemical data indicate that the ﬂuid was hydrothermal in origin, and in addition to causing hematite authigenesis, the ﬂuid also thermally remagnetized pre-existing magnetite in the serpentinite. q 2000 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved. Keywords: remagnetization; ﬂuids; fault; paleomagnetism 1. Introduction In central Scotland, there are numerous exposures of red dolomite in the Caledonian (pre

HBF) in the Lower Paleozoic Highland Border Group (HBG). This study uses paleomagnetic analysis to date the ﬂuid migration event responsible for the dolomitiza- tion in the HBG and to assess whether the dolomite represents a single episode of ﬂuid-ﬂow and alteration of the basement, or if there were multiple events that are juxtaposed coincidentally. 2. Geological setting The trace of the HBF can be mapped with conﬁ- dence for a distance of 230 km from Stonehaven to Arran in central Scotland (Fig. 1). The predominant rocks to the north of the fault are Dalradian metasedi- ments whereas the rocks to the south are continental Devonian (Old Red Sandstone, ORS) sediments. At many places there is a narrow outcrop of the HBG, immediately south of the fault plane. These rocks represent an oceanic or backarc assemblage that has been excised almost completely. It includes several exposures of serpentinite, representing sea-ﬂoor basic rocks altered by meteoric ﬂuids (Ikin and Harmon, 1983). In some outcrops the serpentinite is massive. In others it is brecciated, either due to tectonic activity or synsedimentary processes. Outcrops of the serpentinite exhibit extensive dolo- mitization and/or siliciﬁcation. The alteration occurs partly as a massive replacement and partly as thin (from 1 to ,10 cm)

. Petrographic and geochemical studies are underway to assess this possibility. In summary, the results from the fault zone rocks in the HBF indicate that there was at least one dolomi- tizing and hematite-precipitating ﬂuid alteration event in central Scotland in the late Carboniferous. Measurement of the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility on the gabbroic samples reveals a flat-lying foliation with a radiating pattern of lineations, supporting the field evidence that the gabbros are part of a large, undeformed sill. Petrographic observations of oxides in the gabbros reveals two populations of magnetite grains produced during the original cooling of the sill: large, oxyexsolved titanomagnetite grains and fine-grained magnetite in igneous reaction rims. New 40Ar/39Ar age dating of biotite and plagioclase yield ages of V1.2 Ga, which represent the rapid cooling following emplacement of the mafic magma. A pilot collection (usually 25%–30% of the total number of samples) was randomly selected for each exposure. The pilot collection was subjected to detailed thermal demagnetization, and its results were used to choose an optimum regime of demagnetization, i.e., the temperature at which, supposedly, only the characteristic component remained in the sample. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. The following rejection criteria were employed: small signal values comparable with the instrumentation noise,

DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. The paleomagnetic poles from the study rocks clearly differ from younger poles of the Siberian Platform. All these data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component was acquired at the time of or shortly after the deposition of the Lakhandinskaya Group. Taking into account recent paleomagnetic data on the Middle Riphean Malginskaya Formation, results of this current work suggest, depending on the choice of the paleomagnetic direction polarity, two possible scenarios for relative movements of the Siberian Platform and Laurentia in a 1100–1000-Ma interval. One of these scenarios contradicts the hypothesis on Siberia as a part of the Rodinia supercontinent. The second scenario, which implies a variation in the generally accepted polarity for one of the cratonic blocks considered, is in a good agreement with this hypothesis but requires a coincidence of northern Laurentia with south-southeastern Siberia, rather than with its northern part, as is assumed in most reconstructions. A pilot collection (usually 25%–30% of the total number of samples) was randomly selected for each exposure. The pilot collection was subjected to detailed thermal demagnetization, and its results were used to choose an optimum regime of demagnetization, i.e., the temperature at which, supposedly, only the characteristic component remained in the sample. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. Thus, the available data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component formed during or soon after the deposition of the rocks studied. DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. The paleomagnetic poles from the study rocks clearly differ from younger poles of the Siberian Platform. All these data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component was acquired at the time of or shortly after the deposition of the Lakhandinskaya Group. Taking into account recent paleomagnetic data on the Middle Riphean Malginskaya Formation, results of this current work suggest, depending on the choice of the paleomagnetic direction polarity, two possible scenarios for relative movements of the Siberian Platform and Laurentia in a 1100–1000-Ma interval. One of these scenarios contradicts the hypothesis on Siberia as a part of the Rodinia supercontinent. The second scenario, which implies a variation in the generally accepted polarity for one of the cratonic blocks considered, is in a good agreement with this hypothesis but requires a coincidence of northern Laurentia with south-southeastern Siberia, rather than with its northern part, as is assumed in most reconstructions. A pilot collection (usually 25%–30% of the total number of samples) was randomly selected for each exposure. The pilot collection was subjected to detailed thermal demagnetization, and its results were used to choose an optimum regime of demagnetization, i.e., the temperature at which, supposedly, only the characteristic component remained in the sample. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. The following rejection criteria were employed: small signal values comparable with the instrumentation noise,

DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. The paleomagnetic poles from the study rocks clearly differ from younger poles of the Siberian Platform. All these data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component was acquired at the time of or shortly after the deposition of the Lakhandinskaya Group. Taking into account recent paleomagnetic data on the Middle Riphean Malginskaya Formation, results of this current work suggest, depending on the choice of the paleomagnetic direction polarity, two possible scenarios for relative movements of the Siberian Platform and Laurentia in a 1100–1000-Ma interval. One of these scenarios contradicts the hypothesis on Siberia as a part of the Rodinia supercontinent. The second scenario, which implies a variation in the generally accepted polarity for one of the cratonic blocks considered, is in a good agreement with this hypothesis but requires a coincidence of northern Laurentia with south-southeastern Siberia, rather than with its northern part, as is assumed in most reconstructions.
